prompt: Which two promises of a relational database do NoSQL families most often give up?

choices.text: Any query, and transactions across any rows
choices.why: Right. In exchange for partitioning and replication built in.

choices.text: Replication and partitioning
choices.why: Those are what they gained.

choices.text: Storing several tables per machine
choices.why: Nothing in the families is about how many tables a machine holds.

choices.text: Durability, and indexes
choices.why: Most keep both; durability is configurable and indexes exist in nearly all.

prompt: What does a NoSQL database usually give you that lesson 2 had to build by hand?

choices.text: Joins across shards
choices.why: Joins are what they make expensive.

choices.text: Unlimited multi-row transactions
choices.why: Transactions are usually limited to one item or partition.

choices.text: Data spread across servers by a key
choices.why: Right, with no router in the program.

choices.text: A schema checked on every write
choices.why: Most check less, not more.

prompt: Where does designing for a NoSQL database start?

choices.text: From normalising every fact so it lives in one place only, then writing the queries
choices.why: Normalising first is the relational order; here facts are copied where questions need them.

choices.text: From the product with the most features
choices.why: Products come after the questions.

choices.text: From the entities and their relations
choices.why: That is relational design.

choices.text: From the questions the program will ask
choices.why: Right: access patterns, with how often and how fast.

prompt: What is denormalisation, as the lesson uses the word?

choices.text: Splitting a table into partitions by month
choices.why: That is partitioning, from lesson 2.

choices.text: Removing the schema
choices.why: Schemas are a separate matter.

choices.text: Copying a fact wherever a question needs it
choices.why: Right, and keeping the copies in step in the program.

choices.text: Deleting duplicated rows
choices.why: That is the opposite direction.

prompt: Match each access pattern of the box office to the family that fits it.

pairs.left: hold a seat for ten minutes
everything about one show in one read
door scans by show, in time order
who went to this show also went to…
tickets sold per minute, last month

prompt: Why can a key-value store not answer 'every seat on hold for show 1' by itself?

choices.text: Keys cannot contain a colon
choices.why: The lesson's keys do.

choices.text: It only answers questions about one key
choices.why: Right. A list would have to be kept under another key.

choices.text: Holds expire before they can be listed
choices.why: They last ten minutes; listing is the problem.

choices.text: It would need a transaction across two servers
choices.why: It needs a query over many keys, which the store does not offer.

prompt: Why is partitioning trivial for a key-value store?

choices.text: Keys are sorted, so ranges split cleanly
choices.why: A hash spreads them; it does not sort them.

choices.text: Every server keeps a copy of every key, so any server can answer for any key
choices.why: That would be replication of everything, not partitioning.

choices.text: Values are small enough to fit in one packet
choices.why: Size does not decide where a key lives.

choices.text: No operation involves two keys
choices.why: Right. The key's hash picks one server and nothing else is needed.

prompt: Ana's SET … NX EX 600 answered OK and Bia's, a moment later, answered (nil). What does Bia's program learn?

choices.text: The key expired
choices.why: TTL still showed 600 seconds.

choices.text: Bia's hold replaced Ana's
choices.why: GET afterwards returned ana.

choices.text: The seat is already held
choices.why: Right. NX sets only if the key is absent.

choices.text: The hold failed because of an error
choices.why: (nil) is the normal answer when NX finds the key.

prompt: Two buyers send SET hold:show:1:seat:42 … NX in the same millisecond. Why does exactly one get OK, with no transaction?

choices.text: Redis runs one command at a time, so check and write are one step
choices.why: Right. The command is atomic by construction.

choices.text: Redis locks the key for ten minutes
choices.why: The ten minutes are the expiry; there is no lock.

choices.text: The faster client's packet always arrives first, so its command is checked before the other one starts
choices.why: Arrival order only decides who wins; the guarantee comes from commands not interleaving.

choices.text: EX makes the command transactional
choices.why: EX only sets the lifetime.

prompt: With -P 16, GETs went from about 97 000 to about 1 408 000 a second. What did pipelining remove?

choices.text: Expiry checks on every key read, which a pipeline skips
choices.why: Expiry is checked the same way pipelined or not.

choices.text: Most of the round trips
choices.why: Right. Sixteen commands per trip.

choices.text: The work of looking up each key
choices.why: Each key is still looked up.

choices.text: Writing to disk
choices.why: GETs never write.

prompt: In the capture, what did INCRBY views:show:1 10 answer?
In SET key value NX EX 600, the option that makes the key disappear after 600 seconds is ___ .
Why are a show's tickets kept as separate documents rather than embedded in the show?

choices.text: Embedding would break the show's _id
choices.why: Ids are unaffected by embedding.

choices.text: Documents cannot hold lists
choices.why: The show document holds lists of artists and prices.

choices.text: Tickets need a schema
choices.why: Nothing in the reason is about schemas.

choices.text: They grow without limit and change constantly
choices.why: Right, and they are read one at a time.

prompt: Arena Sul is renamed. What does the embedded design cost?

choices.text: Finding and rewriting every show document at that venue
choices.why: Right. Cheaper reads, harder writes.

choices.text: A migration of the collection's schema, run while every page is closed for maintenance
choices.why: The shape is unchanged; only values change.

choices.text: One update to the venue's row
choices.why: That is the relational cost; here the name is copied.

choices.text: Nothing, because the database propagates it
choices.why: No database checks or updates embedded copies.

prompt: A field is a candidate for embedding. Put the lesson's three tests in the order the table lists them.
items: Is it read with the parent almost every time?
Does it change rarely, or is a stale copy acceptable?

prompt: In PRIMARY KEY ((show_id), scanned_at, ticket), what does scanned_at do?

choices.text: Indexes every scan across all partitions so that any time range can be read without naming a show
choices.why: A query still names one partition; the clustering key orders inside it.

choices.text: Makes each scan expire after a day
choices.why: Nothing in the key sets an expiry.

choices.text: Keeps the rows of a partition sorted by time
choices.why: Right. It is the clustering key.

choices.text: Decides which server holds the row
choices.why: That is show_id, the partition key.

prompt: A new question arrives: every scan at gate B tonight. What does the lesson say is the answer?

choices.text: Add gate to the partition key of the existing table
choices.why: That would break the query by show it was designed for.

choices.text: A second table keyed for it, written alongside
choices.why: Right. One table per query.

choices.text: Filter the existing table by gate
choices.why: That reads every partition; the store refuses it unless forced.

choices.text: Join scans to a gates table
choices.why: The family does not do joins.

prompt: Why do writes stay fast in Cassandra as the data grows?

choices.text: It keeps every partition in memory
choices.why: Data is flushed to files on disk.

choices.text: No write reads anything first
choices.why: Right. Appends to memory and a log, merged later.

choices.text: It modifies files in place
choices.why: Files are never modified, only merged.

choices.text: It skips the commit log
choices.why: It writes to the commit log.

prompt: What makes a graph database cheap at following relationships?

choices.text: It shards the graph by node type
choices.why: Graphs are hard to shard; that is a weakness.

choices.text: It keeps every path precomputed
choices.why: Paths are walked at query time.

choices.text: Relationships are stored as foreign keys
choices.why: That is the relational way, with an index lookup per hop.

choices.text: Each node holds direct references to its relationships
choices.why: Right. No index search per step.

prompt: For which question does a graph database gain the most over SQL?

choices.text: Tickets per minute, with every minute of the year kept and old minutes rolled into hours
choices.why: That is a time-series question.

choices.text: Connections up to six steps away
choices.why: Right. Each extra hop is another self-join in SQL.

choices.text: The buyer of one ticket, found from the ticket's id
choices.why: One hop is a join SQL does well.

choices.text: Total tickets sold this year
choices.why: Counting large sets is where graphs fit poorly.

prompt: Why should a buyer's id not be a tag in a time-series database?

choices.text: Tags must be numbers
choices.why: The lesson's tags are text, like channel=web.

choices.text: Buyers' ids are personal data
choices.why: True, and not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: Every tag value makes a new series, and millions outgrow the index
choices.why: Right. High-cardinality values are fields.

choices.text: Fields cannot be grouped by
choices.why: That is why only a few dimensions should be tags.

prompt: What does downsampling do?

choices.text: Samples a random subset of incoming points so that the database writes less of them
choices.why: It aggregates everything, by time bucket; nothing is random.

choices.text: Deletes every point older than the retention period, partition by partition
choices.why: That is retention; downsampling keeps a summary.

choices.text: Rolls raw points into coarser ones as they age
choices.why: Right, and drops the raw ones.

choices.text: Compresses each point
choices.why: Compression keeps every point.

prompt: In the line sales,show=1,channel=web tickets=3i …, show and channel are tags, and tickets is a ___ .
Which cost of adding a database does the lesson call the worst?

choices.text: The licence
choices.why: Every database in the lessons is free to run.

choices.text: The disk space
choices.why: The lesson does not mention it.

choices.text: Learning its query language
choices.why: Real, and smaller than the operational costs.

choices.text: Keeping its copy of the data in step with the others
choices.why: Right. There is no transaction across databases.

prompt: A team wants documents for show pages. By the lesson's habit, what do they check before adding MongoDB?

choices.text: Whether the other shows' pages need it too
choices.why: It is the same pattern for every show.

choices.text: Whether MongoDB is faster than PostgreSQL in a benchmark published by MongoDB's own company
choices.why: Their own measurement of their own pattern is what decides.

choices.text: Whether jsonb in their PostgreSQL serves the pattern well enough
choices.why: Right. Measured, not assumed.

choices.text: Whether MongoDB can be the source of truth for tickets
choices.why: The question is about show pages.

prompt: A seat hold is kept in Redis and the sale in PostgreSQL. Redis restarts and loses its data. What happens to sales?

choices.text: Every seat becomes double-booked
choices.why: The sale itself still checks PostgreSQL.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses sales until Redis recovers
choices.why: PostgreSQL knows nothing of Redis.

choices.text: Nothing is lost; open holds disappear and buyers hold again
choices.why: Right. Holds are short-lived; the truth of a sale is in PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Sales made during the last ten minutes are lost
choices.why: Sales were never in Redis.

prompt: Which family suits 'every reading of every sensor in a venue, every second, kept a week and then hourly'?

choices.text: Time series
choices.why: Right: retention and downsampling.

choices.text: Key-value, with one key per reading so that each second has its own entry
choices.why: No range reads, no rollups; the wrong shape.

choices.text: Document, one per sensor per day
choices.why: Each reading is not a thing read whole.

choices.text: Graph, with each sensor as a node
choices.why: Nothing here is about connections.
